claims.text: Modest grain-boundary segregation of selected heavy, corrosion-resistant elements enables lightweight high-entropy alloys to combine low density with high mechanical strength, corrosion resistance, and oxidation resistance.
Grain-boundary segregation leads to the in situ formation of stable, thin passivating oxide layers.
The passivating oxide layers shield the alloy surface.
The passivating oxide layers pin grain boundaries and hinder dislocation motion.
A controlled heat treatment or thermomechanical treatment can promote grain-boundary segregation of selected alloying elements.
Enrichment of corrosion-resistant elements at grain boundaries facilitates development of a thin, adherent oxide film.
Local enrichment in protective-oxide-forming elements improves resistance to high-temperature oxidation.
Local enrichment in protective-oxide-forming elements improves resistance to corrosive environments.
Segregation-derived oxide films reinforce mechanical strength by acting as barriers to dislocation motion.
Redistributing alloying elements through segregation can provide these benefits without significantly increasing overall alloy density.
Relative to a homogenized baseline, the segregation-treated alloy should have a lower corrosion rate.
Relative to a homogenized baseline, the segregation-treated alloy should have a lower oxidation rate.
Relative to a homogenized baseline, the segregation-treated alloy should have higher yield strength.
The segregation treatment should not appreciably increase alloy density relative to the baseline.
The proposed mechanism should cease to operate if high temperature destabilizes the protective oxide.
The proposed mechanism should cease to operate if diffusion homogenizes the segregated microstructure.
Excessive segregation can produce brittle intermetallic phases and eliminate the proposed benefit.
A segregation-treated alloy lacking statistically significant improvements in both environmental resistance and mechanical strength relative to the control would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The initial material is described as uniformly mixed, while the baseline is called both 'as-cast' and 'homogenized.' An as-cast state and a post-casting homogenized state are normally distinct processing conditions, so the baseline state is ambiguous.

The passivating oxide is described as a surface-shielding film but is also said to pin grain boundaries and directly impede dislocations. The hypothesis does not specify whether oxide forms at the external surface, internally along grain boundaries, or both, leaving the mechanical role inconsistent with the stated surface-passivation role.
